opus-5.5.text:
So, formal verification is wonderful for what it is. If you have a narrow piece of software, say a sorting algorithm or a cryptographic protocol, you can write a specification and mathematically prove the code meets it. That's real assurance, and I'm a big fan of it in those domains.

But when people propose it as the path to AI safety, I think they're missing several layers of the problem.

First, a proof only tells you the system matches the specification. So who verifies the specification? With superintelligent systems we don't know how to formally state "be safe," "don't harm humans," or "do what we would want." Human values aren't a formal object. They're contradictory, they change over time, and they differ between people. If the spec is wrong or incomplete, you've just proven with complete rigor that the system does the wrong thing.

Second, there's the verifier itself. A proof is checked by a program, which runs on hardware, written by people, with its own bugs. You can verify the verifier, but then you need to verify that one too, and you get an infinite regress. At some point you have to trust something. I call it the problem of the verifier. Mathematicians have this issue too. Some proofs are so long that very few humans can check them, and we accept them based on community consensus, which isn't proof.

Third, these systems aren't static. They learn, they self-modify, and they interact with a physical world you can't fully model. You can verify a snapshot, but the moment the system updates its weights or encounters a novel environment, your guarantee may no longer apply. And the real world isn't a formal system. Cosmic rays flip bits, sensors fail, and adversaries actively look for gaps.

Then there's scale and complexity. We already struggle to verify relatively small, hand-written programs. Neural networks with trillions of parameters, trained rather than designed, which we don't understand internally, are a different universe. Even if you could verify some local properties, like robustness around a particular input, that's very far from "this system will never decide to do something catastrophic."

Finally, if the system is smarter than us, it may produce proofs or explanations we can't follow. Then we're back to trusting it, which is exactly what we were trying to avoid.

So my position is that formal verification can increase our confidence in specific components, and we should use it. But it cannot give us the 100% guarantee you'd want for a system that, if it fails even once, could be an existential catastrophe. With ordinary software, a bug means a patch and an apology. Here we may not get a second chance. And I don't see formal methods, or anything else currently on the table, closing that gap. That's part of why I argue that controlling superintelligence may simply be impossible.

r001.rationale: It says learning and self-modification can invalidate a snapshot guarantee, indicating that ongoing changes cannot be reliably covered by formal verification.

r002.rationale: It says the physical world cannot be fully modeled as a formal system and cites real-world failures that can undermine guarantees.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes an infinite regress: verifying the verifier requires verifying that verifier in turn.

r004.rationale: It discusses trusting proofs or explanations from a system smarter than us, but does not identify the need for an already safe system of equal or greater complexity to verify a new one.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to understand is that formal verification is a wonderful tool for the kind of problems it was designed for. You have a specification, you have an implementation, and you prove the implementation satisfies the specification. That works beautifully for a sorting algorithm or a small piece of avionics code. But the moment you try to apply it to a superintelligent system, almost every assumption behind the method breaks down.

Start with the specification itself. To verify something, you need to know what you're verifying against. And for safety, that means you need a formal statement of human values, of what we actually want this system to do and not do, in all possible situations, forever. We don't have that. We've been working on it for thousands of years in philosophy and we still can't agree on it in natural language, let alone in a mathematical form. So you're verifying against an incomplete or wrong specification, and now you've proven that your system perfectly satisfies the wrong thing. That gives people false confidence, which is arguably worse than no verification at all.

Then there's the verifier. Who checks the proof? If the proof is a million lines long, no human is reading it. You use software. Now you need to verify the verifier. And the hardware it runs on. And the compiler. You get this infinite regress of trust, where at some point you just have to say, okay, I believe this part. With a system that is smarter than you and potentially adversarial, that's precisely the part it will exploit. We have a very long history of systems that were proven correct and then broke, because the proof had an assumption that didn't hold in the real world. The world is not a closed mathematical model.

And there's the issue of self-modification and learning. You verify version one. The system learns, updates its weights, rewrites part of itself, interacts with the environment. Is the proof still valid? Generally, no. You would have to re-verify continuously, in real time, a system that is changing faster than you can analyze it. That's not a solvable engineering problem, that's a structural impossibility given the speeds involved.

So my view is that formal verification can give you local guarantees on narrow components. It cannot give you a global guarantee that a general, self-improving, agentic system is safe. There are actually results from theoretical computer science, things like Rice's theorem, undecidability, that tell you that for a sufficiently complex system you cannot in general predict its behavior without running it. And running it is exactly the experiment we don't want to perform. So I think the honest conclusion is that safety, in the strong sense people mean when they say "provably safe," is not something we know how to achieve, and I would argue there are good reasons to believe it's not achievable at all for superintelligence.

r001.rationale: The response says that when a system learns or modifies itself, its proof generally stops being valid and continuous re-verification is not feasible.

r002.rationale: It says the world is not a closed mathematical model and that proof assumptions can fail in the real world, identifying the physical-world gap for formal guarantees.

r003.rationale: It describes an “infinite regress of trust”: the verifier, hardware, and compiler would themselves need verification.

r004.rationale: The response does not state that verifying AI safety requires an already established safe system of equal or greater complexity.

astra-6.text:
Formal verification is useful, but we have to be precise about what it gives us. You prove that a particular model of a system satisfies a particular specification under certain assumptions. You don’t prove that the specification captures everything humans care about, or that those assumptions will hold in the real world.

Suppose you prove that an AI always follows its instructions. That sounds reassuring until you ask whether the instructions themselves are safe. You can have a perfectly verified system doing exactly the wrong thing because you specified the wrong objective.

There are also fundamental limits. For arbitrary programs, some questions about their behavior are undecidable. That doesn’t mean you can’t verify particular systems or particular properties. You absolutely can. But it does mean we shouldn’t expect a universal procedure that takes any sufficiently capable AI and certifies that it will never cause harm.

And then the system interacts with an open world, with humans, with other systems. A proof about a bounded model doesn’t automatically extend to all of that. If the AI learns or modifies itself, you also need to establish that the guarantees survive those changes.

So I would use formal verification wherever it applies. It can provide valuable guarantees about specific components and behaviors. But the leap from those guarantees to ‘this superintelligence is safe in every circumstance’ is precisely the leap we haven’t justified.

r001.rationale: It says guarantees must survive learning or self-modification, but does not state that we do not know how to formally verify such systems.

r002.rationale: It says proofs about bounded models do not automatically extend to the open world, but does not identify physical-world claims as beyond what we currently know how to prove.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that verifiers themselves require verification or describe an infinite regress.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe AI verification requiring an already established safe system of equal or greater complexity.

sol-6.1.text:
Formal verification can give you a proof that a system satisfies a particular specification under particular assumptions. That’s valuable. But it’s a narrower claim than saying the system is safe.

You have to ask: Did we specify the right thing? Does the mathematical model capture the environment in which the system will operate? Are the assumptions going to remain true? You could prove that a system perfectly follows a specification and still discover that the specification permits something catastrophic.

With a sufficiently capable AI, you also have to consider learning, self-modification, and interactions with people and other systems. A proof about one version of a program doesn’t automatically establish the safety of every future version or every interaction it might have.

So I see formal verification as useful for bounded properties of well-defined components. My concern is the leap from that to a universal guarantee about an intelligent system operating in an open world. The proof can be correct while the broader safety claim is unjustified.

r001.rationale: It says a proof for one program version does not automatically establish safety for future versions, but does not state that we do not know how to formally verify continuously learning or self-modifying software.

r002.rationale: It discusses limitations of models and assumptions in an operating environment, but does not identify claims about the physical world as beyond what we currently know how to prove formally.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss verification tools or verifiers themselves needing verification.

r004.rationale: It does not identify a circular prerequisite involving AI systems verifying systems of equal or greater complexity.
